name: Aqualyx jaw fat-dissolving injections

card.summary: Injections of Aqualyx, a lipolytic product from Marllor Biomedical, into small fat pockets under the chin and jawline to reduce fullness and define the jaw.
card.note: Swelling and bruising are expected; injectable lipolysis is regulated differently by country.

quick.overview:
Aqualyx is an injectable cosmetic product from the Italian company Marllor Biomedical, used in clinics to reduce small fat deposits. For the jaw, it is aimed at fullness under the chin and along the jawline, with the goal of a sharper-looking jaw and neck profile.

The better-known related approach is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), approved by the US FDA in 2015 for fat below the chin. Published research specific to Aqualyx at the jaw is not included here, so the description relies on the manufacturer and on broader injection-lipolysis references.
quick.how: Treatment is performed by a clinician in a clinic, generally as small injections into the targeted fat, with the body clearing the treated fat over time. Typically several weeks to months are involved before the final contour shows.
quick.risks: Injection lipolysis commonly causes bruising, swelling and pain. Mesotherapy-style injections have drawn regulatory scrutiny in some countries, including bans in parts of South America and infections reported in Australia; a French ban was later lifted after problems were attributed to hygiene.

lead: Aqualyx jaw fat-dissolving injections are clinic treatments in which Aqualyx, a product of Marllor Biomedical, is injected into small localised fat to reduce fullness. Marllor describes itself as an Italian company founded in 2009 by Dr Pasquale Motolese and Vania Bedetti, and lists Aqualyx Cosmetic among its products.[1]

Applied to the jaw area, the aim is to reduce submental fullness (the 'double chin') and soften jowl fat so the jawline looks more defined. A closely related, regulated alternative is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), FDA-approved in April 2015 for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin.[2][3]
Mesotherapy-type injections are described as aiming to cause lipolysis and adipocyte death, though critics say cosmetic uses have not undergone standard clinical trials.[3]

chain: Injection into chin and jaw fat
Treated fat cells are cleared over weeks
Slimmer chin area and sharper jaw outline
angle.text: Reducing the fat layer below the chin and along the jaw can make the jawline and neck angle more visible. People pursue it as a non-surgical alternative to liposuction.

paras: Marllor Biomedical was founded in Italy in 2009 and sells Aqualyx Cosmetic.[1] Injection lipolysis more broadly has used detergent-like compounds such as sodium deoxycholate, sometimes with phosphatidylcholine.[2]

Deoxycholic acid was approved by the FDA for submental fat in 2015; a generic has been available in the US since April 2021.[2] Mesotherapy generally has been criticised by some dermatologists and plastic surgeons as insufficiently studied. Some South American countries banned it, and Australian cases of abscesses and an atypical mycobacterial infection were reported; France's 2011 ban on fat-removal use was later lifted after investigators attributed problems to unhygienic conditions.[3]

No studies found for Aqualyx at the jaw. For deoxycholic acid, a phase III trial supporting FDA approval reported a 68.2% response, with about 81% having mild, temporary side effects such as bruising, swelling and pain.[3] A 2025 mouse study of a different herbal injection, LIPOSA-T, examined localised fat reduction.[4]

timeline.event: FDA approves deoxycholic acid for submental fat.[2][3]
